# Correlation and Linear Regression

## Correlation

Pearson measures **linear** association; Spearman and Kendall measure **monotonic** association.

```r
loc  <- c(120, 340, 88, 410, 200, 75, 510, 290, 130, 360)
bugs <- c(  2,   7,  1,   9,   4,  0,  12,   6,   3,   8)

cor(loc, bugs)
cor(loc, bugs, method = "spearman")
cor.test(loc, bugs)
```

**Correlation is not causation.** Confounders (project age, complexity, team size) might explain both LOC and bugs.

## Simple Linear Regression

The model: $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.

```r
fit <- lm(bugs ~ loc)
summary(fit)
confint(fit)
```

## Diagnostics

Linear regression has four key assumptions: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of residuals.

```r
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fit)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## Transformations

```r
fit_log <- lm(log(bugs + 1) ~ log(loc))
summary(fit_log)
```

## Prediction Intervals vs. Confidence Intervals

```r
new <- data.frame(loc = c(200, 500))
predict(fit, new, interval = "confidence")
predict(fit, new, interval = "prediction")
```

The prediction interval is always wider because it includes both estimation uncertainty and irreducible noise.
